hmmt-feb-2024-team-01.title: Complete the square
hmmt-feb-2024-team-01.body:
Clearing the denominator, $\sum a_i^2=100\sum a_i$, i.e. $\sum(a_i^2-100a_i)=0$, which is
$$(a_1-50)^2+(a_2-50)^2+\cdots+(a_{100}-50)^2=100\cdot50^2=500^2.$$
Hence $(a_1-50)^2\le500^2$ and $a_1\le550$. Equality holds for $a_1=550$, $a_2=\cdots=a_{100}=50$: then $\sum a_i^2=550^2+99\cdot2500=550000$ and $\sum a_i=5500$, ratio $100$.

The maximum is $550$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-01.title: Cauchy–Schwarz and a one-variable minimum
hmmt-feb-2024-team-01.body:
Let $k=\frac1{99}(a_2+\cdots+a_{100})$. By Cauchy–Schwarz, $a_2^2+\cdots+a_{100}^2\ge99k^2$, so with $t=a_1$ (we may assume $t>0$; the denominator is positive since the numerator is),
$$100\ge\frac{t^2+99k^2}{t+99k}.$$
For fixed $t>0$ the function $f(x)=\frac{t^2+99x^2}{t+99x}$ on $x>-\frac t{99}$ has derivative zero where $(t+99x)^2=100t^2$, i.e. at $x=\frac t{11}$ (the root in the domain), where $f=\frac{2t}{11}$; this is its minimum. Hence $\frac{2t}{11}\le100$, so $a_1\le550$, with equality at $(550,50,\dots,50)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-02.title: Which four cells can show 23
hmmt-feb-2024-team-02.body:
Write the grid as
$$\begin{matrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{matrix}\quad\longrightarrow\quad\begin{matrix}b+d&a+c+e&b+f\\a+e+g&b+d+f+h&c+e+i\\d+h&e+g+i&f+h\end{matrix}$$
- Two corners on the same side cannot both be $23$: e.g. $b+d\ne b+f$ since $d\ne f$.
- Two edge cells sharing a corner cannot both be $23$: e.g. $a+c+e\ne a+e+g$ since $c\ne g$.
- The center cannot be $23$: its new value $b+d+f+h$ exceeds each new corner value (e.g. $b+d$), so no corner would be $23$, and then three edge cells would have to be $23$ — but among any three edge cells two share a corner.

So the four $23$'s are two opposite corners and two opposite edge cells, and (by the first two rules) they must be arranged as, up to symmetry, the new values at $a,b,h,i$:
$$92=(b+d)+(a+c+e)+(e+g+i)+(f+h)=(a+b+\cdots+i)+e=74+e,$$
so $e=18$.

**Example.** The grid with rows $4,16,2$ / $6,18,7$ / $1,17,3$ (sum $74$, all distinct) becomes rows $22,24,23$ / $23,46,23$ / $23,22,24$, with exactly four $23$'s.

The only possible center is $18$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-03.title: Congruent triangles at $M$
hmmt-feb-2024-team-03.body:
Let $Y$ be the intersection of lines $AB$ and $XM$. Since $BY\parallel CX$, $\angle YBM=\angle XCM$; also $BM=CM$ and $\angle BMY=\angle CMX$ (vertical angles). So $\triangle BMY\cong\triangle CMX$ and $MY=MX$.

Thus $AM$ is a median of triangle $AYX$ that is also perpendicular to $YX$ (since $\angle AMX=90^\circ$). So $AY=AX$ and $AM$ bisects $\angle YAX$, which is the same angle as $\angle BAX$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-03.title: Reflect $A$ through $M$
hmmt-feb-2024-team-03.body:
Let $A'$ be the reflection of $A$ over $M$, so $ABA'C$ is a parallelogram and $CA'\parallel AB$. Then $A'$ lies on the line through $C$ parallel to $AB$, which also contains $X$.

In triangle $AXA'$, the line $XM$ is perpendicular to $AA'$ and passes through its midpoint $M$, so $XA=XA'$ and $\angle XAA'=\angle XA'A$. Since $A'X\parallel AB$, alternate angles give $\angle XA'A=\angle BAA'$. Hence $\angle XAM=\angle BAM$: $AM$ bisects $\angle BAX$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-04.title: Mod 3 structure, a bound, and a construction
hmmt-feb-2024-team-04.body:
Let $\ell(x,y)$ be the label.

**Divisible by 3.** For all $x,y$ the labels $\ell(x,y),\ell(x,y+1),\ell(x+1,y)$ are distinct mod $3$. Then $\ell(x+1,y+1)$ differs mod $3$ from both $\ell(x+1,y)$ and $\ell(x,y+1)$, so $\ell(x+1,y+1)\equiv\ell(x,y)$. Next, $\ell(x,y+1),\ell(x,y+2),\ell(x+1,y+1)$ are distinct mod 3 and $\ell(x+1,y+1)\equiv\ell(x,y)$, so $\ell(x,y),\ell(x,y+1),\ell(x,y+2)$ are distinct mod 3; consequently $\ell(x,y+3)\equiv\ell(x,y)$. Similarly in the $x$-direction. Combining, $\ell(w,x)\equiv\ell(y,z)\pmod3$ whenever $w-x\equiv y-z\pmod3$. As $2000-2024\equiv0\equiv0-0$, $\ell(2000,2024)\equiv0\pmod3$.

**At most 6048.** Moving one step right or up changes a label by at most $2$ (three consecutive numbers). Then $\ell(x+1,y+1)\le\ell(x,y)+4$, and being $\equiv\ell(x,y)$ mod 3 it is at most $\ell(x,y)+3$. So $\ell(2000,2000)\le3\cdot2000$ and $\ell(2000,2024)\le6000+2\cdot24=6048$.

**Construction.** Let $L_m$ be the line $x+2y=m$; $(2000,2024)$ lies on $L_{6048}$. The points $(x,y),(x,y+1),(x+1,y)$ lie on three consecutive lines $L_m,L_{m+1},L_{m+2}$ ($m=x+2y$) in some order. For a multiple of $3$, $k\ge0$, label every point of $L_m$ by $\max(m\bmod3,\ m-k)$, which is $m\bmod3$ for $m\le k$ and $m-k$ for $m\ge k$. Three consecutive lines $L_m,L_{m+1},L_{m+2}$ then get labels $\{0,1,2\}$ if $m+1\le k$, and $\{m-k,m-k+1,m-k+2\}$ if $m\ge k$ — always three consecutive numbers — and $(0,0)$ gets $0$. The label of $(2000,2024)$ is $\max(0,6048-k)$, which takes every multiple of $3$ from $0$ to $6048$ as $k$ ranges over $0,3,\dots,6048$.

The possible labels are $0,3,6,\dots,6048$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-05.title: How to find it
hmmt-feb-2024-team-05.body: Since $x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)$, it is enough that $x+y$, $x^2+y^2$ and $x^2-xy+y^2$ are squares. Try $x=a(a+b)$, $y=b(a+b)$: then $x+y=(a+b)^2$, $x^2+y^2=(a+b)^2(a^2+b^2)$ and $x^2-xy+y^2=(a+b)^2(a^2-ab+b^2)$. So we need $a^2+b^2$ and $a^2-ab+b^2$ to be squares. Among Pythagorean pairs, $(a,b)=(8,15)$ works: $64+225=17^2$ and $64-120+225=169=13^2$. This gives $(x,y)=(8\cdot23,15\cdot23)=(184,345)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-06.title: Show $f$ is linear
hmmt-feb-2024-team-06.body:
Let $P(x,y)$ denote the equation. $P(x,0)$: $f(f(x))=x+af(0)$. Applying $f$ to this and using it again, $f(x+af(0))=f(f(f(x)))=f(x)+af(0)$.

$P(f(x),y)$: $f(f(f(x))+ay)=af(y)+f(x)$, i.e. $f(x+af(0)+ay)=f(x)+af(y)$. Replacing $x$ by $x-af(0)$ and using the shift identity:
$$f(x+ay)=f(x)+af(y)-af(0).$$
With $x=0$: $f(ay)=af(y)+(1-a)f(0)$. Substituting back, $f(x+ay)=f(x)+f(ay)-f(0)$ for all $x,y$, so $g(x)=f(x)-f(0)$ is additive on $\mathbb Q$, hence $g(x)=bx$, and $f(x)=bx+c$.

Substituting: $f(ay+bx+c)=aby+b^2x+bc+c$ must equal $a(by+c)+x$, i.e.
$$(b^2-1)x+(b+1-a)c=0\quad\text{for all }x.$$
So $b=\pm1$ and $(b+1-a)c=0$. Since $a\ne0$, $b+1-a=0$ only when $b=1$, $a=2$. Therefore: $f(x)=x$ and $f(x)=-x$ always work; and if $a=2$, every $f(x)=x+c$ works. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-06.title: Via bijectivity
hmmt-feb-2024-team-06.body:
From $f(f(x))=x+af(0)$, $f$ is surjective (the right side takes all rational values) and injective (equal $f$-values give equal $x$). So $f$ is a bijection.

Let $z=f^{-1}(0)$. $P(z,y/a)$ gives $f(y)=af(y/a)+z$. $P(f(x),y/a)$ gives $f(f(f(x))+y)=af(y/a)+f(x)$, i.e. $f(x+af(0)+y)=f(x)+f(y)-z$. Putting $y=0$ shows $f(x+af(0))=f(x)+f(0)-z$, so replacing $x$ by $x-af(0)$ yields $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)-f(0)$. Hence $f(x)-f(0)$ is additive, $f$ is linear, and we conclude as before: $f(x)=\pm x$, plus $f(x)=x+c$ when $a=2$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-07.title: Law of cosines
hmmt-feb-2024-team-07.body:
$AD$, $BE$, $CF$ are diameters of the circumcircle and $P$ is inside it, so each angle is obtuse, or straight when $P$ lies on that diagonal (then its tangent is $0$, consistent with the formula below). Let the side be $1$, $O$ the center, $OP=x<1$, $\theta=\angle AOP$.

By the law of cosines, $AP^2=x^2+1-2x\cos\theta$, $DP^2=x^2+1+2x\cos\theta$, and with $AD=2$:
$$\cos\angle APD=\frac{2(x^2+1)-4}{2\sqrt{(x^2+1)^2-4x^2\cos^2\theta}}=\frac{x^2-1}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)^2+4x^2\sin^2\theta}},$$
so $\sin\angle APD=\frac{2x|\sin\theta|}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)^2+4x^2\sin^2\theta}}$ and
$$\tan\angle APD=\frac{2x|\sin\theta|}{x^2-1}.$$
The diagonals $BE$, $CF$ make angles $\theta+60^\circ$, $\theta+120^\circ$ with $OP$ (directed), so the three tangents are $\frac{2x}{x^2-1}$ times
$$|\sin\theta|,\quad|\sin(\theta+60^\circ)|,\quad|\sin(\theta+120^\circ)|.$$
Since $\sin\theta+\sin(\theta+120^\circ)=2\sin(\theta+60^\circ)\cos60^\circ=\sin(\theta+60^\circ)$, the signed values $u,v,w$ satisfy $u-v+w=0$; whatever their signs, one of $|u|,|v|,|w|$ is the sum of the other two. Multiplying by the common factor, two of the tangents sum to the third. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-07.title: Coaxial circles
hmmt-feb-2024-team-07.body:
Let $O$ be the center and the side be $1$. $O$ has equal power $AO\cdot OD=BO\cdot OE=CO\cdot OF$ with respect to the circles $(APD)$, $(BPE)$, $(CPF)$, and $P$ lies on all three, so the circles are coaxial with radical axis $OP$. Their centers $X,Y,Z$ therefore lie on one line (perpendicular to $OP$). Also $XO\perp AD$, $YO\perp BE$, $ZO\perp CF$, so consecutive lines $OX,OY,OZ$ make $60^\circ$ angles. WLOG $Y$ is between $X$ and $Z$ with $\angle XOY=\angle YOZ=60^\circ$; then $OY$ bisects the $120^\circ$ angle $XOZ$, and the bisector length formula gives $OY=\frac{2\,OX\cdot OZ\cos60^\circ}{OX+OZ}$, i.e. $\frac1{OY}=\frac1{OX}+\frac1{OZ}$.

Finally $\angle APD=180^\circ-\frac12\angle AXD=180^\circ-\angle AXO$, so $\tan\angle APD=-\tan\angle AXO=-\frac{AO}{OX}=-\frac1{OX}$; similarly $\tan\angle BPE=-\frac1{OY}$, $\tan\angle CPF=-\frac1{OZ}$. The relation above says two of the tangents sum to the third. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-08.title: Radical axis with an auxiliary circle
hmmt-feb-2024-team-08.body:
Equal radii and a common chord give equal inscribed angles: chord $PA$ of the congruent circles $(PDA)$ and $(PAB)$ gives $\angle PDA=\angle PBA$, and chord $PB$ of $(PAB)$ and $(PBC)$ gives $\angle BCP=\angle PAB$ (with the appropriate orientation; directed angles $\measuredangle$ mod $180^\circ$ below).

Let $A'$ be the second intersection of line $PA$ with circle $(PDX)$, and $B'$ the second intersection of $PB$ with $(PCX)$. Point $A$ lies on lines $DX$ and $PA'$, so its power with respect to circle $(PDA'X)$ is $AD\cdot AX=AP\cdot AA'$. The first product is also its power with respect to $(XCD)$, and the second its power with respect to $(PA'B')$. So $A$ has equal power with respect to $(XCD)$ and $(PA'B')$; similarly for $B$ via $(PCB'X)$. Hence $AB$ is the radical axis of $(PA'B')$ and $(XCD)$, and the line of their centers is perpendicular to $AB$.

Now
$$\measuredangle PA'X=\measuredangle PDX=\measuredangle PDA=\measuredangle ABP,\qquad\measuredangle XB'P=\measuredangle XCP=\measuredangle BCP=\measuredangle PAB.$$
Together with $\measuredangle B'PA'=\measuredangle BPA$, this shows $A',X,B'$ are collinear and $\triangle PAB\sim\triangle PB'A'$ (antiparallel). Hence the $P$-altitude of $\triangle PAB$ passes through the circumcenter of $\triangle PA'B'$ (circumcenter and orthocenter are isogonal conjugates, and $A'B'$ is antiparallel to $AB$).

So the center of $(PA'B')$ lies on the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$, and the center $O$ of $(XCD)$ lies on the perpendicular to $AB$ through that center — the same line. Thus $OP\perp AB$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-08.title: Reflection across the $P$-altitude
hmmt-feb-2024-team-08.body:
Since the circles have equal radii, $\angle PDA=\angle ABP$. If $(PDA)$ meets line $AB$ again at $B'$, then $\angle PB'B=\angle PBB'$, so $PB'=PB$; likewise the second intersection $A'$ of $(PCB)$ with $AB$ satisfies $PA'=PA$. Thus $(PDA)=(PAB')$ and $(PCB)=(PBA')$ are mirror images in the $P$-altitude $h$ of $\triangle PAB$.

Let $C'$ be the reflection of $C$ in $h$. It suffices to show $C'$ lies on $(XCD)$: then the center of $(XCD)$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $CC'$, which is $h$, so $OP\perp AB$.

By the mirror symmetry, $C'$ lies on $(PDA)$. Now $C'CBB'$ is an isosceles trapezoid ($C'B'$ is the reflection of $CB$ in $h$), so
$$\angle C'DA=180^\circ-\angle C'B'A=180^\circ-\angle C'B'B=\angle C'CB=\angle C'CX,$$
using that $C',D,A,B'$ are concyclic. Hence $C'DXC$ is cyclic, i.e. $C'\in(XCD)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-09.title: Ring bound and a matching construction
hmmt-feb-2024-team-09.body:
Let $n=100$ (grid $2n\times2n$). Each car moves straight until it exits, so the total number of moves is $\sum_c d(c)$, where $d(c)$ is the distance from the car to the edge in its direction (counting the exit move); it does not depend on the order.

**Upper bound.** Split the grid into concentric square rings $S_1$ (border), …, $S_n$ (central $2\times2$). Fix $S_k$.
- A corner car of $S_k$ has $d(c)\le2n+1-k$.
- A non-corner car at $(x,k)$ (with $k<x<2n+1-k$) pairs with the opposite car at $(x,2n+1-k)$; they cannot face each other (neither could ever pass the other), so $d(c)+d(c')\le(2n+1-k)+\max(x,2n+1-x)$. Similarly for the other pair of sides.
- Consider the first car to leave the square formed by $S_k,\dots,S_n$: it lies on $S_k$ and points straight outward, so $d(c)=k$, and its pair then satisfies $d(c)+d(c')\le2n+1$, which is at least $n+1-k$ below the bound above.

Summing,
$$\sum_{c\in S_k}d(c)\le4(2n+1-k)+4\sum_{x=k+1}^{n}\big[(2n+1-k)+(2n+1-x)\big]-(n+1-k),$$
and summing over $k=1,\dots,n$ gives $\frac12n(12n^2+3n-1)$.

**Construction.** Number rows $1,\dots,2n$ from the bottom. Upper-left quadrant: all cars face down; upper-right: left; lower-left: right; lower-right: up; except that the right half of row $n$ (the top row of the lower half) faces right. Clear it by: removing all of row $n$; then for $k=n-1,\dots,1$ moving the $n$ upward cars of row $k$ one step and removing the rest of row $k$; then clearing the upper-left, upper-right and lower-right quadrants in turn. Its total is $4\cdot\frac{n^2(3n+1)}2-\frac{n(n+1)}2=\frac12n(12n^2+3n-1)$, so the bound is attained.

For $n=100$: $\frac12\cdot100\cdot(120000+300-1)=6014950$. (A computer search confirms the maximum $7$ for the $2\times2$ grid, and the construction is clearable with total $53$ for the $4\times4$ grid, matching the formula.) ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-10.title: $p$-adic continuity and a construction
hmmt-feb-2024-team-10.body:
**Claim.** $P(i)$ can be exactly the numbers $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$ and $v_p(a),v_p(b)\ge0$ for every prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$.

Integer-valued polynomials are exactly $\sum_k c_k\binom xk$ with $c_k\in\mathbb Z$, so $P$ has rational coefficients and $P(i)=a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$, and $P(-i)=a-bi$.

**Necessity.** Fix $p\equiv1\pmod4$. Then $x^2+1=0$ has a root in the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb Z_p$, so $\pm i\in\mathbb Z_p$. Choose integers $m_k\to i$ in $\mathbb Z_p$; then $-m_k\to-i$. By continuity of polynomials, $P(m_k)+P(-m_k)\to2a$ and $P(m_k)-P(-m_k)\to2bi$. The left sides are integers, which have nonnegative $p$-adic valuation, and $\mathbb Z_p$ is closed, so $v_p(2a),v_p(2bi)\ge0$, i.e. $v_p(a),v_p(b)\ge0$ ($p$ odd, $i$ a $p$-adic unit).

**Sufficiency.** The set of attainable values is closed under addition and multiplication (sums/products of integer-valued polynomials) and contains $\mathbb Z[i]$ (linear polynomials). So it suffices to obtain $\frac1p$ for each prime $p\not\equiv1\pmod4$.
- $p=2$: $P(x)=\frac14x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)+3=6\binom x4+3$ is integer-valued, and $i(i-1)(i-2)(i-3)=(-1-i)(5-5i)=-10$, so $P(i)=-\frac{10}4+3=\frac12$.
- $p\equiv3\pmod4$: $\binom ip=\frac{i(i-1)\cdots(i-p+1)}{p!}$. Its numerator $N=i(i-1)\cdots(i-p+1)$ has $N\bar N=\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}(1+j^2)$, which is not divisible by $p$ since $-1$ is not a square mod $p$; so $(p-1)!\binom ip=\frac Np=\frac{a+bi}p$ with $p\nmid a^2+b^2$. Multiplying by $a-bi$ gives $\frac{a^2+b^2}p$ with $p\nmid a^2+b^2$, and by Bézout (combining with integers) $\frac1p$ is attainable.

Hence the possible values are exactly as claimed. ∎

hmmt-feb-2024-team-10.title: Necessity via Gaussian integers
hmmt-feb-2024-team-10.body:
As above write $P=\sum c_k\binom xk$, $c_k\in\mathbb Z$. It suffices to show that for each $k$ and each prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$, $p$ does not divide the denominator of $\binom ik$ in $\mathbb Q(i)$.

In $\mathbb Z[i]$, $p=\pi\bar\pi$ with Gaussian primes $\pi,\bar\pi$. We need
$$v_\pi\big(i(i-1)\cdots(i-k+1)\big)\ge v_\pi(k!)=\Big\lfloor\frac kp\Big\rfloor+\Big\lfloor\frac k{p^2}\Big\rfloor+\cdots$$
(and the same for $\bar\pi$, by conjugation).

**Key claim.** For $t\ge1$, among any $p^t$ consecutive numbers $i-n-1,\dots,i-n-p^t$ one is divisible by $\pi^t$. Indeed, by Hensel's lemma there is $s$ with $p^t\mid s^2+1=(s-i)(s+i)$; since $\gcd(s-i,s+i)\mid2$, $\pi^t$ divides $s-i$ or $s+i$, so $\pi^t\mid i-r$ for $r=\pm s$; the block contains an $n+x\equiv r\pmod{p^t}$.

So among $i,i-1,\dots,i-k+1$, at least $\lfloor k/p^t\rfloor$ factors are divisible by $\pi^t$ for each $t$, which gives the inequality. The construction for sufficiency is as in the first solution. ∎
